items.title: Saturday 80s Jam: I Still Haven’t Found What I’m Looking for – U2
items.author: Schill
items.content:
When U2 released “I Still Haven’t Found What I’m Looking For” in 1987, they were already one of the biggest rock bands of the decade. But the song represented another step forward for a group that had spent much of its career trying to expand the possibilities of what a rock band could sound like.

Released as the second single from , the song was built around a deceptively simple idea: the search for something meaningful that never quite ends. It could be interpreted as a love song, a spiritual reflection, or a statement about ambition and dissatisfaction. That ambiguity helped make it one of U2’s most enduring recordings.

The song began with a very different musical foundation than the finished version. Drummer Larry Mullen Jr. had been experimenting with a rhythm that producer Daniel Lanois and the band developed into something with a distinctive gospel influence. Guitarist The Edge then created the shimmering, echo-heavy guitar sound that became one of the recording’s defining characteristics.

The result was unlike much of the arena rock dominating the 1980s.

It was big without being bombastic.

The rhythm was steady and hypnotic, while The Edge’s guitar seemed to float above the arrangement. Then Bono’s voice entered, delivering the song with a mixture of certainty and doubt.

That contradiction is central to the recording.

The singer is searching, but he hasn’t arrived.

He has experienced love, traveled, struggled, believed, doubted, and continued moving forward, yet something remains unresolved. The song never provides a neat answer.

That made it particularly powerful.

“I Still Haven’t Found What I’m Looking For” became one of U2’s biggest American hits, reaching number one on the Billboard Hot 100. It also became a major international success and helped become one of the defining albums of the 1980s.

The song’s gospel influence was especially notable. U2 had incorporated religious imagery throughout their career, but here the connection between rock music and gospel was unusually direct. The backing vocals and arrangement gave the song a spiritual atmosphere without turning it into a conventional religious recording.

Then there was Bono’s performance.

Rather than singing the song like a traditional rock anthem, he gradually increases the emotional intensity. His voice sounds both powerful and vulnerable, perfectly matching the central idea of someone who continues searching despite never finding exactly what they want.

The song also represented the evolution of U2’s sound during the 1980s. They had started the decade as a relatively straightforward post-punk band from Dublin. By 1987, they were making expansive, atmospheric rock that incorporated American blues, gospel, roots music, and experimental production.

was the culmination of that development.

“I Still Haven’t Found What I’m Looking For” was one of the clearest examples of how far they had come.

It wasn’t built around a flashy guitar solo or a complicated arrangement. Instead, its power came from atmosphere, repetition, vocal performance, and an idea almost everyone can understand.

The feeling that you’ve accomplished something but still aren’t quite where you want to be.

That feeling doesn’t belong to 1987.

More than three decades later, the song remains one of U2’s signature recordings and one of the defining rock songs of the late 1980s. Its combination of rock, gospel, and atmospheric production helped broaden the sound of mainstream rock while giving U2 one of their most enduring songs.

And perhaps the most interesting thing about the title is that it never promises the search will end.

And somehow, that uncertainty is exactly what makes the song so powerful.

items.title: Humpday Hottie: Paige Spiranac
items.author: Schill
items.content:
Paige Spiranac is an American former professional golfer, social media personality, and sports media figure who became one of the most recognizable personalities in golf. Born in Wheat Ridge, Colorado, in 1993, she grew up in an athletic family and initially pursued gymnastics before focusing on golf.

Spiranac played college golf at the University of Arizona and San Diego State University, where she competed at the collegiate level. She later played professionally on developmental golf tours, including the Cactus Tour, where she recorded a victory in 2016. Although her professional playing career was relatively brief, her visibility outside traditional tournament golf grew rapidly.

Spiranac became particularly well known through social media, where she combined golf instruction, entertainment, and commentary. Her videos and posts attracted a huge audience, making her one of the most-followed golf personalities online. Her approach was different from traditional golf media, emphasizing accessibility and entertainment alongside the sport itself.

She has also worked as a golf commentator, podcast host, and content creator. Her media career has included interviews with professional golfers, instructional material, equipment discussions, and coverage of major golf events.

One of the defining aspects of Spiranac’s career has been her role in discussions about how golf is presented to younger and more casual audiences. She has frequently used humor and an informal presentation style rather than the more traditional tone associated with golf broadcasting.

Spiranac has also spoken publicly about the criticism and online attention that accompanied her rise to prominence, particularly the way female athletes and sports personalities are treated on social media.

Whether discussing golf technique, professional tournaments, equipment, or the culture surrounding the sport, Spiranac has built a career that extends well beyond competitive golf. Her transition from collegiate and professional golfer to a major digital media personality illustrates how social media has changed the traditional boundaries of sports celebrity.

items.title: The Cars – “You Might Think” vs. Huey Lewis & the News – “The Power of Love”
items.author: Schill
items.content:
The 1980s produced an incredible number of pop-rock songs that managed to be commercially successful, musically distinctive, and permanently attached to the decade’s cultural identity. Two outstanding examples are The Cars’ “You Might Think” and Huey Lewis & the News’ “The Power of Love.” Both songs arrived during the golden age of MTV, both became defining hits for their respective artists, and both demonstrated how a great hook could turn a straightforward rock song into a pop-culture institution.

Released in 1984, “You Might Think” showcased The Cars’ ability to combine new wave eccentricity with polished, radio-friendly songwriting. A year later, “The Power of Love” became one of the signature songs of the era, pairing Huey Lewis’s energetic vocals with a driving rock arrangement that practically demanded to be played at maximum volume.

One song is quirky, sophisticated, and unmistakably new wave. The other is muscular, exuberant, and built around the kind of chorus that can fill an arena. Which deserves the crown? Let’s put them through ten rounds of musical combat.

Song Spotlight: The Cars – “You Might Think”

Appearing on the 1984 album , “You Might Think” captures The Cars at their commercial and creative peak. Ric Ocasek’s songwriting combines nervous romantic obsession with a playful melody, while the band’s trademark blend of synthesizers, electric guitars, and precise rhythms gives the track its distinctive character.

The production is bright and meticulously arranged, but the song never feels sterile. The guitars provide a satisfying crunch, the keyboards add a futuristic sheen, and the rhythm section keeps everything moving. Ocasek’s understated vocals are central to the appeal. Rather than delivering an oversized rock performance, he sounds like someone casually explaining a ridiculous situation, which makes the song’s eccentricity even more effective.

The accompanying music video became a landmark of the MTV era, using imaginative visual effects and surreal transformations to match the song’s offbeat personality. “You Might Think” was more than another successful single; it was an example of how The Cars could make unconventional ideas sound completely accessible.

Song Spotlight: Huey Lewis & the News – “The Power of Love”

Released in 1985, “The Power of Love” became one of Huey Lewis & the News’ biggest hits and an essential part of the soundtrack. The song’s success was no accident. Its opening guitar riff establishes an immediate sense of momentum, the rhythm section drives the arrangement forward, and Huey Lewis delivers the vocals with the confidence of a frontman who understands exactly how to command a crowd.

The band’s blend of rock, pop, and R&B gives the song a muscular, celebratory quality. Everything feels designed to build toward that enormous chorus, which remains one of the most instantly recognizable hooks of the decade.

Its connection to Marty McFly’s adventures helped give the song a cultural life beyond the charts. Yet “The Power of Love” is more than a movie tie-in. It is a superbly constructed rock single that showcases the band’s ability to make polished, accessible music without sacrificing energy.

Round 1: The Opening Hook

“You Might Think” immediately establishes its identity through bright keyboards, crisp guitars, and a melody that feels slightly off-kilter in the best possible way. The Cars waste no time getting to the song’s infectious central idea, and the arrangement keeps the listener engaged through its carefully placed instrumental details.

“The Power of Love” counters with a chunky guitar riff that announces itself with considerably more muscle. Its groove is direct, confident, and immediately recognizable. Huey Lewis and the News know how to make a song sound enormous without overcomplicating the arrangement.

Both openings are excellent, but The Cars offer a more distinctive combination of sounds and melodic personality.

Round Winner: The Cars – “You Might Think.”

Round 2: Vocal Performance

Ric Ocasek’s vocal delivery is an essential part of The Cars’ identity. His slightly detached, conversational style gives “You Might Think” an unusual charm. He never sounds like he is trying too hard, and that restraint makes the song’s obsessive romantic perspective amusing rather than melodramatic.

Huey Lewis takes the opposite approach. His voice is fuller, bluesier, and more forceful, bringing a natural enthusiasm to “The Power of Love.” He sounds like a frontman who could deliver the song to a packed stadium and have every person singing along by the second chorus.

Ocasek is perfectly suited to his song, but Lewis demonstrates greater vocal power and range of expression.

Round Winner: Huey Lewis & the News – “The Power of Love.”

The chorus of “You Might Think” is a master class in economical pop songwriting. Its central hook is simple enough to remember after one listen, but the melody has enough personality to avoid sounding generic. The Cars make the refrain feel playful, slightly obsessive, and effortlessly catchy.

“The Power of Love” delivers a more explosive chorus. The arrangement opens up, the vocal becomes more commanding, and the song takes on the feeling of a full-scale celebration. It is the sort of refrain that works equally well on the radio, in a movie, or in front of thousands of concertgoers.

The Cars have the more eccentric hook, but Huey Lewis and the News deliver the bigger payoff.

Round Winner: Huey Lewis & the News – “The Power of Love.”

Round 4: Instrumentation and Musicianship

The Cars excel at making every instrument serve the song. The guitars and synthesizers complement one another rather than competing for attention, while the rhythm section provides a precise foundation. The production allows individual details to emerge without disrupting the track’s forward momentum.

“The Power of Love” relies on a more traditional rock arrangement, but that approach is executed exceptionally well. The guitar work gives the song its backbone, the bass and drums establish an irresistible groove, and the band sounds completely comfortable in its chosen style.

This is a close contest between precision and propulsion. The Cars’ arrangement is more distinctive, and its interplay between keyboards and guitars gives the song a slight advantage in musical character.

Round Winner: The Cars – “You Might Think.”

Produced by Robert John “Mutt” Lange, “You Might Think” benefits from the sleek, meticulously controlled sound that defined . Every instrument occupies its own space, the vocals remain clear, and the synthesizers add atmosphere without overwhelming the guitars. The result is a polished recording that still retains The Cars’ personality.

“The Power of Love” sounds equally comfortable in its own sonic environment. Its production emphasizes punch, clarity, and momentum. The guitar riff cuts through the mix, the drums provide a strong foundation, and the chorus feels appropriately oversized without becoming cluttered.

Both recordings are superb examples of mid-1980s studio craft. However, “You Might Think” integrates its electronic and rock elements with slightly greater originality.

Round Winner: The Cars – “You Might Think.”

The Cars had already established a recognizable sound by the time “You Might Think” arrived, but the song still feels unusual. Its combination of nervous romantic subject matter, deadpan vocals, bright keyboards, and angular pop-rock arrangements gives it an identity that few other bands could convincingly reproduce.

“The Power of Love” is an outstanding example of mainstream rock songwriting, but its ingredients are more familiar. A commanding guitar riff, a strong vocal, a driving rhythm, and an enormous chorus are classic components of the genre. Huey Lewis and the News execute them brilliantly, yet the song is less adventurous in its construction.

Originality is where The Cars establish a meaningful advantage. Their song sounds like a world of its own rather than simply a particularly good example of a familiar formula.

Round Winner: The Cars – “You Might Think.”

Round 7: Music Video and Visual Impact

“You Might Think” became one of the defining videos of early MTV, embracing computer-generated imagery and surreal visual effects at a time when the technology was still relatively novel. The bizarre transformations and playful imagery perfectly complemented the song’s personality. The video also won Video of the Year at the inaugural MTV Video Music Awards in 1984.

“The Power of Love” benefits from its association with . The movie connection gives the song a narrative and cultural context that has helped it remain recognizable across generations. It is an effective promotional video and a memorable piece of 1980s entertainment.

Nevertheless, The Cars delivered the more groundbreaking visual experience. Their video was not simply a way to sell a single; it helped expand the creative possibilities of the medium.

Round Winner: The Cars – “You Might Think.”

“You Might Think” was a major hit and an important part of The Cars’ commercial peak. Its music video helped establish the band as an MTV-era powerhouse, and the song remains closely associated with the sound and style of mid-1980s pop-rock.

“The Power of Love” has an especially powerful cultural advantage: . The song became inseparable from one of the decade’s most beloved films, giving it exposure to audiences who might never have discovered Huey Lewis & the News through radio alone. Its chart success and enduring movie association have kept it firmly embedded in popular culture.

The Cars made the more innovative artistic statement, but the combination of a major hit and a legendary film gives Huey Lewis the edge here.

Round Winner: Huey Lewis & the News – “The Power of Love.”

Round 9: Longevity and Replay Value

“You Might Think” remains a highly enjoyable listen because its appeal extends beyond nostalgia. The arrangement contains enough little details to reward repeated listening, and the song’s unusual personality prevents it from becoming just another dated artifact of the MTV era.

“The Power of Love” has tremendous replay value as well. Its direct songwriting, infectious groove, and association with make it an easy choice for classic-rock playlists, movie-themed events, and nostalgic listening sessions. The chorus is as effective today as it was in 1985.

Both songs have aged remarkably well. The Cars win narrowly because their more distinctive arrangement gives listeners additional musical details to appreciate with repeated plays.

Round Winner: The Cars – “You Might Think.”

Round 10: The Ultimate Feel-Good Factor

“You Might Think” is fun in a slightly strange, intellectually playful way. Its melody is infectious, its lyrics have a humorous edge, and its arrangement creates an atmosphere of bright, quirky optimism. It is the kind of song that makes you appreciate the wonderfully odd things that mainstream pop music could accomplish in the 1980s.

“The Power of Love” is pure, uncomplicated exhilaration. The groove makes you want to move, the chorus invites everyone to sing along, and the performance radiates confidence. It is tailor-made for road trips, parties, and those moments when a familiar song instantly improves the atmosphere.

The Cars make you smile, but Huey Lewis and the News make you want to turn up the volume and sing along at the top of your lungs.

Round Winner: Huey Lewis & the News – “The Power of Love.”

The final score is The Cars 6, Huey Lewis & the News 4.

“You Might Think” takes the overall victory by offering the more distinctive musical identity. Its inventive arrangement, carefully controlled production, memorable melody, and groundbreaking video make it a particularly strong representation of what made 1980s pop-rock so exciting. The Cars understood how to combine commercial songwriting with an eccentric streak that kept their music from sounding ordinary.

“The Power of Love” puts up an impressive fight. Huey Lewis delivers the stronger vocal performance, the bigger chorus, and the more immediately celebratory listening experience. Its connection to also gives it an enduring cultural advantage that few singles can match.

Ultimately, this battle comes down to innovation versus pure rock-and-roll exhilaration. Huey Lewis and the News made the kind of song that could unite an entire room, while The Cars created a track with a little more personality and a sound that remains uniquely their own.

The Winner: The Cars – “You Might Think.”

Sometimes the best song isn’t the loudest or the biggest hit. Sometimes it’s the one that manages to be catchy, strange, sophisticated, and completely irresistible all at once.

items.title: Saturday 80s Jam: How Will I Know – Whitney Houston
items.author: Schill
items.content:
When Whitney Houston released “How Will I Know” in 1985, she was still in the early stages of what would become one of the most extraordinary careers in pop music. Her debut album had already produced “You Give Good Love,” but “How Will I Know” was the song that showed the world just how perfectly her enormous voice could fit into bright, energetic 1980s pop.

Written by George Merrill, Shannon Rubicam, and Narada Michael Walden, the song was originally intended for another artist. Houston’s version transformed it into something much bigger. Produced by Michael Walden, the recording combined synthesizers, electronic drums, handclaps, keyboards, and a relentlessly upbeat rhythm that was almost impossible to sit still through.

That was a major departure from the more serious image often associated with powerhouse vocalists.

Houston could obviously sing a huge ballad, but “How Will I Know” demonstrated that she could also have fun.

The song is essentially about romantic uncertainty. Houston is interested in someone but doesn’t know whether the feelings are mutual. Instead of treating that uncertainty as something dramatic and depressing, the song turns it into a burst of nervous energy.

The production is a huge part of that feeling.

The drums bounce along, the keyboards sparkle, the backing vocals reinforce the chorus, and Houston’s voice cuts through the arrangement with astonishing clarity. She doesn’t have to overpower the production. She simply sits perfectly on top of it.

Directed by Brian Grant, the “How Will I Know” video was filled with bright colors, geometric sets, dancers, energetic choreography, and unmistakable mid-1980s fashion. It was tailor-made for MTV, which was rapidly becoming one of the most important promotional forces in popular music.

Houston’s image in the video was youthful, stylish, and playful.

She wasn’t being presented solely as a serious vocalist standing behind a microphone. She was a pop star.

The song became Houston’s second number-one single on the Billboard Hot 100 and helped turn her debut album into a massive success. It also established a formula that would define much of her early career: combine an extraordinary voice with sophisticated pop production and make the result accessible to virtually anyone.

“How Will I Know” is particularly impressive because Houston never sounds like she’s struggling to fit into the upbeat production.

She sounds completely natural.

Her vocal runs add personality without overwhelming the melody, while the chorus gives her plenty of room to show off the power that would eventually become her trademark.

The song also captures something essential about 1980s pop. This was the decade when electronic production, MTV, fashion, dance music, and traditional vocal performances increasingly came together.

“How Will I Know” sits right in the middle of that cultural shift.

It sounds unmistakably like 1985, but its melody is strong enough that the song never feels trapped in its era.

Most importantly, it helped establish Whitney Houston as something more than a promising new singer.

She was becoming a superstar.

Over the next several years, Houston would deliver enormous ballads, blockbuster movie songs, and some of the most recognizable recordings in popular music.

But “How Will I Know” remains special because it captures her at the beginning of that journey.

Young, energetic, impossibly talented, and surrounded by one of the decade’s most infectious productions, Whitney Houston turned a song about wondering whether someone liked her into a celebration of the excitement of not knowing.

And the answer, judging by the success of the song, was pretty obvious.

Everybody was going to know Whitney Houston.

items.title: Forgotten Band: Icicle Works
items.author: Schill
items.content:
There are plenty of forgotten bands from the 1980s that make you wonder how they ever disappeared. Then there are bands like The Icicle Works, where the question becomes even more frustrating:

How did a band this good have only one song that everybody remembers?

If you were listening to alternative radio in the early 1980s, you probably remember “Whisper to a Scream (Birds Fly).” It was catchy, energetic and just strange enough to stand apart from the endless parade of synth-heavy new wave that was filling radio stations.

The song was a legitimate hit.

And that’s a shame, because The Icicle Works had a much more interesting story than their one familiar song suggests.

They came from Liverpool, England, created a sound that mixed post-punk, new wave, progressive rock and straight-up pop, and produced several albums that deserve far more attention than they receive today.

They were never quite weird enough to be completely underground and never quite commercial enough to become superstars.

That awkward middle ground is where a lot of forgotten bands ended up.

From Liverpool to the World

The Icicle Works were formed in Liverpool in the early 1980s by singer, guitarist and songwriter Ian McNabb.

McNabb was the creative force behind the band, and his songwriting immediately separated The Icicle Works from many of their contemporaries.

The band wasn’t interested in simply copying the synth-pop formula.

There were keyboards and electronic textures, but there were also jangly guitars, driving rhythms and surprisingly ambitious arrangements.

The music could sound bright and upbeat while still having a slightly melancholy edge.

That combination fit perfectly into the early-1980s British alternative scene.

Liverpool already had a remarkable musical history, and The Icicle Works became part of another generation of musicians trying to figure out what came after punk.

The answer, for them, was to take the energy of punk and combine it with ambitious pop songwriting.

The song that changed everything was “Whisper to a Scream (Birds Fly).”

The title alone sounded like something you’d find printed on an early-’80s import single.

The song itself was even better.

It started with a distinctive rhythmic pulse before opening into jangling guitars and McNabb’s urgent vocals.

It was catchy without sounding disposable.

The song eventually became a significant hit in the United States, reaching the Top 40, and suddenly The Icicle Works had an opportunity to become much bigger.

For a brief moment, they looked like they might be one of the British bands capable of breaking through in America.

That didn’t quite happen.

Which is a shame, because they had the songs.

The band’s 1984 debut album, , is where anyone rediscovering the group should start.

It’s much more than a vehicle for “Whisper to a Scream.”

The album demonstrates just how adventurous McNabb could be as a songwriter.

There are atmospheric passages, energetic guitar-driven songs, electronic touches and big melodic choruses.

The band could shift from moody to explosive without losing its identity.

It’s very much an early-’80s record, but it doesn’t feel trapped in the decade.

That’s an important distinction.

A lot of new wave records now sound like museum pieces.

The Icicle Works still sounds like a band.

They Were More Than New Wave

Calling The Icicle Works a new wave band isn’t necessarily wrong, but it’s incomplete.

They had too many different influences.

There were progressive-rock ideas.

There was folk and psychedelic influence.

There were enormous pop melodies.

McNabb wasn’t afraid to experiment with song structures either.

That made the band difficult to categorize.

And once again, that’s probably part of the reason they never became huge.

The 1980s music industry loved easy descriptions.

The Icicle Works could fit into several of those categories without completely belonging to any of them.

The band continued with albums including and If You Want to Defeat Your Enemy Sing His Song.

The latter title alone should tell you something about McNabb.

He wasn’t exactly thinking in terms of three-minute radio formulas.

The albums continued to demonstrate that the band had plenty of ideas beyond their biggest American hit.

There were moments of experimentation alongside straightforward pop-rock.

Unfortunately, the commercial momentum wasn’t enough to turn The Icicle Works into a household name.

They became one of those bands that had a recognizable song without becoming a recognizable band.

That’s a particularly strange form of musical fame.

The Icicle Works benefited from MTV during the era when British bands were flooding American television.

The visual presentation of “Whisper to a Scream” helped the song stand out.

But MTV also created an interesting problem.

It could make a song famous much faster than it could make an entire catalog famous.

A viewer might see the video, remember the chorus, and move on to the next band.

That’s essentially what happened.

The Icicle Works became associated with one song.

The rest of the catalog disappeared behind it.

Ian McNabb Never Really Stopped

One of the biggest misconceptions about forgotten bands is that they disappeared because they had nothing left to say.

That wasn’t the case with Ian McNabb.

After The Icicle Works’ original run, McNabb continued recording and performing, including solo work and later incarnations of the band.

He remained an active musician while The Icicle Works became increasingly associated with nostalgia for the 1980s.

That’s another reason the group is worth rediscovering.

They’re not simply a historical curiosity.

There is a substantial body of music behind the one song most people remember.

The Icicle Works suffered from terrible timing.

They arrived during an extraordinary period in British music.

There were so many great bands that even genuinely talented groups could get lost.

You had The Cure, New Order, The Smiths, Echo & the Bunnymen, Simple Minds, U2, Tears for Fears, The Psychedelic Furs, The English Beat, The Church and dozens of others competing for attention.

That’s a ridiculous amount of competition.

A band could have a hit and still disappear from the larger cultural memory.

The Icicle Works did exactly that.

They became a footnote in a decade packed with musical stories.

The Great Thing About Rediscovering Them

The Icicle Works are one of those bands where the rediscovery process is genuinely rewarding.

You start with “Whisper to a Scream.”

You think, “Oh yeah, I remember this.”

Then you listen to the first album.

Wait a minute. These guys were actually really good.

And there are more songs.

More ambitious arrangements.

More of Ian McNabb’s excellent songwriting.

That’s the fun of forgotten bands.

You’re not discovering some obscure group that nobody liked.

You’re discovering a band that was good enough to have been much bigger but got lost in the shuffle.

They Deserve More Than One Song

The Icicle Works aren’t completely forgotten.

Their biggest song still turns up on ’80s playlists, radio retrospectives and new wave compilations.

But the band behind that song deserves to be remembered.

They weren’t a one-hit novelty.

They weren’t simply another synth-pop act.

They were a talented Liverpool band with a distinctive sound, a gifted songwriter and a willingness to experiment.

“Whisper to a Scream” may have been their ticket into the mainstream, but it shouldn’t be the end of the journey.

If that’s the only Icicle Works song you know, you’ve heard the introduction.

Now listen to the albums.

Because once you do, you’ll probably have the same reaction that happens with so many forgotten bands:

“How the hell did I forget these guys?”

And that might be the best reason of all to bring The Icicle Works back into the conversation.

They don’t need nostalgia.

They just need somebody to press play.
